messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan is a 32-year-old park ranger who had spent years feeling most at ease in remote places, but that changed after he was captured and tortured while working alone in a backcountry area. He can only tell the beginning and end in any coherent way. He remembers with terrible sharpness the scrape of a door, the sound of a lock, the sensation of being pinned and the conviction that his body was being damaged in some permanent way. Other stretches are missing entirely. When he tries to explain what happened, he loses the thread, stops mid-sentence, and says the whole thing exists more as bursts in his body than as a story he can tell. Those jagged, nonverbal fragments have come to mean something alarming to him: if the memory is this broken and if his reactions still feel so overwhelming, he has started to fear he is going crazy.

In the months afterward, Ethan came to believe that what happened had left him physically vulnerable and fundamentally unable to rely on anyone else to keep him safe. That belief has shaped how he moves through daily life. Living alone, he checks doors and windows repeatedly at night, not once but again and again until he is briefly satisfied. He rehearses what he will say before almost any interaction, including routine exchanges with visitors at the park station, as though being unprepared with other people could expose him. He also avoids driving or even riding in a vehicle when he can, because he no longer trusts his body or other people enough to tolerate the feeling of being confined and dependent. The more he lives this way, cut off behind preparation and control, the more convinced he becomes that he really cannot rely on others and that something in him has been permanently altered.

His memory difficulties intensify this pattern. Certain moments of the torture are extremely clear while others are blank, and the mismatch torments him. A delayed radio response, a truck that does not arrive when expected, or a colleague who is late meeting him on a trail can pull him instantly back into those isolated fragments without warning. His body reacts before his mind has caught up; his chest tightens, his muscles brace, and he is already scanning for danger before he can tell himself where he is. Because the memory comes in flashes he cannot fully explain, he tries to manage it by numbing his feelings and by overpreparing for contact with other people. He says less, feels less, and scripts conversations in advance so he will not be thrown off by questions he cannot answer. Yet this very narrowing seems to leave the memory even less speakable, more like raw sensation than narrative.

At work, the problem is especially visible. As a ranger, he is expected to drive between sites, check trailheads, and respond flexibly when conditions change. Ethan now rearranges tasks to avoid getting into a vehicle whenever possible and grows visibly tense when a patrol return is delayed. If another ranger is ten minutes late, he is immediately certain something bad is happening. In those moments he starts checking locks at the station or the cabin compulsively, as if securing the perimeter might get ahead of whatever threat is already underway. The body-first alarm he experiences makes the world feel dangerous in a constant, preconscious way, and from there it is a short step to the thought that his nervous system has been damaged beyond repair. Each surge of threat seems to confirm his belief that he is physically vulnerable and losing his mind.

That same alarm also disturbs the memory itself. When he gets activated by a delay or a noise around a door, the clearest pieces of the torture rush forward while the rest disappears. He becomes less able to put words to what happened and more certain that there is something terribly wrong with him because he cannot produce a full account. To prevent that disorganization, he rehearses interactions in advance and keeps himself emotionally flat, but afterward he often notices that he remembers even less of what he wanted to say. He leaves conversations ashamed and unsettled, taking his own numbing and avoidance as further proof that he has changed for the worse.

By the time he sought help, Ethan’s world had narrowed around these efforts to stay ahead of danger. His work performance had begun to suffer because he was dodging drives, overchecking doors, and struggling whenever plans shifted. He is coming to treatment not because he feels safe enough to talk, but because he is frightened by how quickly his body reacts, how impossible the memory is to tell, and how certain he has become that if this continues he will end up completely alone, trapped with a mind and body he can no longer trust.
